title: Global warming threatens rice harvests more than crop models predict, study warns
byline: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research
excerpt: A new study on how rising temperatures will affect rice production in Science Advances compares 214 observations from field-warming experiments with seven crop models, revealing modeled estimates for yield reductions from 1°C of global warming were roughly half those of the real-world observed experiments (3.8% instead of 8.1%). The study was led by the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research with contributions from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK).
content_html:
A new study on how rising temperatures will affect rice production in Science Advances compares 214 observations from field-warming experiments with seven crop models, revealing modeled estimates for yield reductions from 1°C of global warming were roughly half those of the real-world observed experiments (3.8% instead of 8.1%). The study was led by the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research with contributions from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK).

Rice is a staple food for more than half of the world's population, but estimates of how climate change will affect production vary widely. One reason is that many scientific assessments do not clearly distinguish between the more gradual effects of higher average temperatures and acute damage caused by heat extremes.

Extreme heat drives the losses

In the new study, results from 214 observed experiments show that extreme heat (exposure to temperatures above 30°C) is the dominant factor behind rice yield losses from warming. At more than 70% of observed sites, high-temperature exposure accounted for more than half of absolute yield change.

However, when compared with seven crop models, the models were shown to be less sensitive to heat extremes than the real-world observations.

"The discrepancy between the observations and models appears to arise mainly because many current crop models don't yet capture heat damage in rice's reproductive stages well. Observations in the study show this is exactly when rice is particularly vulnerable to extreme heat, as panicles and grains develop," commented lead author Yiwei Jian from the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research.

Loss estimates rise sharply

After correcting the models in line with the observed data, the study estimates that an increase of 1°C in global mean temperature would reduce global rice yields by an average of 8.1%. This is approximately twice the loss previously estimated by the crop models (3.8%). The authors stress that their estimates isolate temperature effects and should therefore not be interpreted as a complete forecast of future rice production.

"This is a really significant jump for the models and emphasizes the role of heat extremes in projected losses, not just average temperatures. This intuitively makes sense—when we check the weather in summer to know how to cope with heat, we're looking for the daily high, not the average temperature," commented PIK scientist Christoph Müller, another author of the study.

Biggest revisions in Asia

The study also rethinks the geographical distribution of crop losses. The biggest revisions are in South and Southeast Asia, where rice crops have high exposure to extreme heat. For Pakistan, India and Bangladesh, the yield-loss estimate increases from 2.1% to 6.6%. For Thailand, the Philippines and Myanmar, it increases from 3.7% to 7.7%.

The authors highlight the importance of adaptation measures for rice production that protect crops at their reproductive stage, such as developing and adopting heat-tolerant varieties, adjusting planting dates, optimizing irrigation practices and improving soil quality.

Publication details

Yiwei Jian et al, Vulnerability to high temperature shapes global warming impacts on rice yield, Science Advances (2026). DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed9226. www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aed9226

content_html_zh:
《科学进展》中一项关于气温上升将如何影响水稻产量的新研究将田间变暖实验的 214 项观察结果与七种作物模型进行了比较，揭示了全球变暖 1°C 产量减少的模型估计值大约是现实世界观察到的实验结果的一半（3.8%，而不是 8.1%）。 该研究由亥姆霍兹环境研究中心领导，波茨坦气候影响研究所 (PIK) 也做出了贡献。

大米是世界上一半以上人口的主食，但对气候变化将如何影响生产的估计差异很大。 原因之一是，许多科学评估没有清楚地区分较高平均气温的渐进影响和极端高温造成的急性损害。

极端高温导致损失

在这项新研究中，214 项观察实验的结果表明，极端高温（暴露在 30°C 以上的温度下）是气候变暖造成水稻产量损失的主导因素。 在超过 70% 的观测地点，高温暴露造成了绝对产量变化的一半以上。

然而，与七种作物模型相比，这些模型对极端高温的敏感度低于现实世界的观测结果。

“观察结果和模型之间的差异似乎主要是因为许多当前的作物模型尚未很好地捕捉水稻繁殖阶段的热损伤。 研究中的观察结果表明，此时水稻特别容易受到极端高温的影响，因为穗和谷粒会发育，”亥姆霍兹环境研究中心的第一作者简一伟评论道。

损失预估大幅上升

根据观测数据修正模型后，研究估计，全球平均气温每升高1°C，全球水稻产量将平均减少8.1%。 这大约是作物模型之前估计的损失 (3.8%) 的两倍。 作者强调，他们的估计孤立了温度影响，因此不应被解释为对未来水稻产量的完整预测。

“这对于模型来说是一个真正重大的跳跃，并强调了极端高温在预计损失中的作用，而不仅仅是平均温度。 这直观上是有道理的——当我们检查夏季天气以了解如何应对炎热时，我们寻找的是每日最高温度，而不是平均温度，”该研究的另一位作者、PIK 科学家 Christoph Müller 评论道。

亚洲最大的修订

该研究还重新思考了农作物损失的地理分布。 变化最大的是南亚和东南亚，这些地区的水稻作物经常遭受极端高温的影响。 对于巴基斯坦、印度和孟加拉国，产量损失预估从 2.1% 上升至 6.6%。 泰国、菲律宾和缅甸则从 3.7% 上升至 7.7%。

作者强调了水稻生产适应措施的重要性，这些措施在繁殖阶段保护作物，例如开发和采用耐热品种、调整种植日期、优化灌溉措施和改善土壤质量。
